title: 6.4 External and Individual Factors Influencing Adaptations to Aerobic Endurance Training

cards.front: What acute physiological adjustments occur at elevations greater than 3,900 feet (1,200 m) to compensate for lower atmospheric oxygen pressure?
cards.back: Immediate adjustments include hyperventilation (primarily via increased breathing frequency) and a 30% to 50% surge in submaximal cardiac output driven entirely by elevated heart rate while stroke volume remains constant or slightly reduced.

cards.front: What chronic physiological and metabolic adaptations occur during prolonged altitude acclimatization (3 to 6 weeks at 2,200 to 3,000 m)?
cards.back:
Longer-term acclimatization produces:
  • 30% to 50% increase in red blood cell production
  • 5% to 15% increase in hemoglobin formation
  • Increased pulmonary oxygen diffusing capacity and capillarization
  • Renal excretion of HCO3- to maintain acid-base balance

cards.front: Why does hyperoxic breathing during rest intervals offer limited ergogenic benefit for healthy individuals at sea level?
cards.back: At sea level, healthy individuals breathing ambient air already exhibit an arterial hemoglobin oxygen saturation of 95% to 98%, leaving minimal headroom for additional oxygen transport.

cards.front: What immediate anatomical and physiological impairments in the respiratory tract are caused by cigarette smoking?
cards.back: Nicotine causes bronchiole constriction and paralyzes respiratory cilia, impairing fluid and particle removal and causing debris to accumulate, which increases airway resistance and respiratory strain.

cards.front: How does carbon monoxide from cigarette smoke impair oxygen transport and cardiovascular function during exercise?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide has a much higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin. This reduces arterial oxygen-carrying capacity and triggers elevated catecholamine release, raising resting and submaximal heart rate and blood pressure.

cards.front: How do blood doping and erythropoietin (EPO) administration affect maximal oxygen uptake and submaximal exercise kinetics?
cards.back: Blood doping increases maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) by up to 11% and lowers submaximal heart rate and blood lactate while elevating blood pH due to increased red blood cell oxygen-carrying capacity.

cards.front: What severe medical risks are associated with artificial red blood cell elevation and high hematocrit from blood doping or EPO abuse?
cards.back: High hematocrit dramatically increases blood viscosity, elevating the risk of serious embolic events including stroke, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism, alongside arterial hypertension.

cards.front: How does an individual's genetic potential affect the magnitude of training adaptations as an athlete advances?
cards.back: Each biological system has a genetic upper limit. As athletes approach their genetic ceiling, training gains follow a curve of diminishing returns, where even minute performance improvements (e.g., 0.05%) require precise program design.

cards.front: What physiological changes account for the decline in maximal aerobic power with advancing age in adults?
cards.back: Age-related declines in aerobic power stem primarily from sarcopenia (loss of muscle mass and strength) alongside an increase in relative body fat mass.

cards.front: How do aerobic power values in women compare to age-matched men, and what physiological factors account for this difference?
cards.back: Aerobic power in age-matched women ranges from 73% to 85% of male values. This difference is driven by women's lower blood hemoglobin levels (14 vs. 15–16 g/dL), higher body fat percentage, and smaller heart chamber size and blood volume.
